scenario: Almost every generative recommendation paper today is built around SIDs. Once the user history goes in, the model generates the next item's code one position at a time. Each paper targets one weak point in that chain. HERO finds that distillation passes the teacher's preference for popular items on to the student, and fixes it on 1688 with two teachers. UAGR puts value signals such as shares and full views into both the codes and the beam search scoring, and is fully deployed at Kuaishou. Another paper finds that the good results beam search misses are all lost at the first step, so it moves width to that step. ACT goes further and gives every creator its own token, avoiding SID collisions altogether. The common lesson is that how SIDs are built and how beam search prunes matter as much as the model itself.

papers.title: Diverse-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhipeng Yi, Xinyu Lin, Minxuan Shan, Zipeng Chen, Yujiao Zhao, Chuanyu Xu, Wenjie Wang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation generates the semantic ID (SID) of the next item from a user's interaction history. Existing training objectives mainly supervise target SID tokens, while on-policy distillation (OPD) provides denser supervision through a teacher's probability distribution over all tokens for more effective and efficient training. However, OPD can aggravate popularity bias: teacher feedback favors popular-item tokens, transferring this preference to the student, while student rollout favors popular items, leaving unpopular-item SID paths rarely generated and supervised. These two sources of bias reinforce each other and reduce recommendation diversity. We propose HERO, a diversity-aware OPD framework. Heterogeneous teacher distillation trains two teachers specializing in popular and unpopular items and routes each training sample to the teacher matching the popularity group of its ground-truth item. The student learns from the routed teacher's probability distribution along its own generated SIDs. Diversity-aware item rollout incorporates ground-truth SIDs of unpopular items into training, covering SID paths that the student rarely generates. Only the student is used for inference. Offline experiments on an industrial dataset and three public datasets further demonstrate its effectiveness, diversity, and robustness. Moreover, we deploy HERO in the "Guess What You Like" module on the 1688 homepage, where a 15-day online A/B test shows a 3.412% increase in gross merchandise value (GMV).
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), where the student generates on its own and a teacher gives a full probability distribution at each position, makes generative recommenders train faster, but the student drifts further and further toward popular items. The bias comes from two places: the teacher's probabilities already favor the SIDs of popular items, and the student rarely generates the SIDs of unpopular items, so those paths get almost no supervision. HERO trains a popular-item teacher and an unpopular-item teacher. Each training example goes to the teacher that matches the group of the item the user actually clicked, and the true SIDs of unpopular items are also sent to the unpopular-item teacher. Only the student is served. In a 15-day A/B test on the Guess What You Like module of the 1688 homepage, GMV rose 3.412%.

papers.title: Utility-Aware Generative Recommendation: Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes and Utility-Guided Decoding
papers.authors: Yang Hu, Duo Wang, Ning Li, Kang Li, Junda She, Chengcheng Guo, Kuo Cai, Bin Liu, Youhua Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation has been widely adopted in large-scale industrial recommendation systems, where multimodal item embeddings are quantized into offline semantic identifiers (SIDs) and items are retrieved by autoregressively generating their SIDs. However, conventional SID construction often underrepresents item utility reflected in post-exposure behaviors such as shares, long views, and video completion, making semantically similar items with different utility insufficiently distinguishable while struggling to accommodate rapidly changing utility signals. Moreover, generation likelihood may be misaligned with downstream utility, causing high-utility candidates to be prematurely pruned during beam search before post-generation reranking or training-time reward alignment can effectively compensate. To address these limitations, we propose UAGR, which aligns both SID construction and decoding with downstream multi-objective utility. Our Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes preserve the original semantic information while incorporating item-level utility without increasing SID length or vocabulary size, supporting incremental utility updates with no additional tokenization or sequence-decoding cost. Meanwhile, our Utility-Guided Decoding estimates candidate utility by combining predictions of multiple post-exposure outcomes and incorporates these estimates into beam scoring, reducing the risk of prematurely pruning high-utility paths while enabling flexible utility control without interfering with generative backbone training. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B tests under real-world traffic demonstrate the effectiveness and deployability of UAGR, which has been fully deployed on Kuaishou and increases video watch time by 0.206\% online.
papers.summary: This Kuaishou paper adds video utility to two places in generative recommendation that used to look only at content and probability. 3 bits inside the last SID token record which of 8 tiers the video falls into by a historical utility statistic such as click rate. At every beam-search step a small module reads the decoder hidden state, predicts behaviors such as watching and liking for each candidate, and adds the resulting utility score to the pruning score. This is needed because common generative recommenders build SIDs from content alone, so a video people usually finish and one most people swipe away get nearly the same code whenever their content is similar. Beam search then prunes by generation probability alone, so a high-utility candidate can be cut at some middle token, and later reranking cannot bring it back. It is fully deployed at Kuaishou, lifting video watch time by 0.206%. ==Utility used at the pruning step works better than utility used only for reranking after generation==.

papers.title: Large Language Model as Universal Retriever in Industrial-Scale Recommender System
papers.authors: Junguang Jiang, Yanwen Huang, Liu Bin, Xiaoyu Kong, Xinhang Li
papers.abstract: In real-world recommender systems, different retrieval objectives are typically addressed using task-specific datasets with carefully designed model architectures. We demonstrate that Large Language Models (LLMs) can function as universal retrievers, capable of handling multiple objectives within a generative retrieval framework. To model complex user-item relationships within generative retrieval, we propose multi-query representation. To address the challenge of extremely large candidate sets in industrial recommender systems, we introduce matrix decomposition to boost model learnability, discriminability, and transferability, and we incorporate probabilistic sampling to reduce computation costs. Finally, our Universal Retrieval Model (URM) can adaptively generate a set from tens of millions of candidates based on arbitrary given objective while keeping the latency within tens of milliseconds. Applied to industrial-scale data, URM outperforms expert models elaborately designed for different retrieval objectives on offline experiments and significantly improves the core metric of online advertising platform by $3\%$.

papers.summary: Recommendation retrieval is usually split by objective into several channels, such as collaborative retrieval, long-tail retrieval and interest exploration, each with its own data and model. A team at Alibaba's Taobao and Tmall Group finds that one large language model can handle all of them and still beat the dedicated model of each channel. The input states in one sentence what this retrieval is for, and the model directly generates a set of items from tens of millions of candidates, with latency kept within tens of milliseconds. Beyond the offline comparison, on an online advertising platform it raised the core metric, advertising revenue, by 3%. ==One model that switches retrieval objectives on instruction== can save the cost of maintaining many separate channels.

papers.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuosheng Liu, Yihan Wu, Ziyun Xu, Xiaoxuan Liu, Longfei Yun, Kevin Han, Mingze Gao, Pengfei Wang, Junfeng Pan, Wenjie Fu, Haoran Liu
papers.abstract: Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.
papers.summary: This Meta paper gives every creator its own token in the language model's vocabulary and uses it in place of the SID. The reason is simple: an SID is a many-to-one code, so several creators share one SID, and even when the model generates the right SID it still has to guess which of those creators the user wants. On Meta's creator recommendation data, swapping only the token layer lifts the share of cases where the user's next engaged creator appears in the top 15 from 23.58% to 43.41%. The SID pipeline's per-user inference cost is about 2.7 times the new method's. ==The bottleneck is the SID layer, not the language model==. The price is that every token needs enough training examples, so the authors use it only for head creators.

papers.title: Where Beam Search Loses Top-Ranked Items:First-Step Coverage in Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation can reproduce a wider beam's ranked output with roughly half the prefix-capacity budget by reallocating retention capacity across semantic-ID positions. We identify a \emph{first-step coverage bottleneck}: across six full-test settings of the TIGER generative recommender spanning three domains and two identifier constructions, every pruned exact top-10 path is first lost at the initial decoding step. An exact-catalog reference isolates search losses and guides a controlled budget intervention. Moving width to the first step raises Search Recall@10 by 0.96--10.90 percentage points at Beam-50's unchanged budget. Across all 77,373 test users with residual-quantized variational autoencoder (RQ-VAE) tokenization, the reallocated schedule reproduces Beam-100's ordered top-10 at nominal budgets of 151 rather than 301, without retraining or changing identifiers or scores. Matched-output timing saves 6.35--6.39\% of decoder latency; profiling identifies the execution costs that limit the translation from reduced search work to runtime savings. Larger-candidate experiments reveal how output size changes retention requirements. These findings make budget placement an actionable serving decision: locate ranking loss, redirect search capacity, and preserve downstream inputs before increasing uniform beam width.
papers.summary: A generative recommender uses beam search to produce a SID one token at a time, and the usual way to miss fewer good results is to widen every step at once. This paper checks six full-test settings of TIGER one by one: every result that the model's own scores put in the top 10, but that beam search pruned, was lost at the very first step. So the cheaper move is to concentrate width on the first step and narrow the later ones. With this allocation, about half the prefix budget (the total number of prefixes kept across steps) reproduces the top 10 of a beam twice as wide, in the same order, with no retraining. ==Beam width should go to the step where results get lost==.

papers.title: Think Globally, Generate Personally: Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yuxuan Hu, Yingyi Zhang, Wenlin Zhang, Chao Zhang, Haotian Nan, Ziwei Liu, Jiancheng Dong, Tongzhou Wu, Beibei Kong, Lei Cheng, Chengxiang Zhuo, Zang Li, Wanyu Wang, Xiangyu Zhao
papers.abstract: Semantic-ID-based (SID) generative recommendation (GR) represents each item as a sequence of discrete tokens and predicts the next item through autoregressive SID generation. However, existing methods face two challenges. First, insufficient shared context modeling for user sequences: full-history and recent behaviors provide overlapping yet complementary evidence, but modeling them within a single sequence may dilute current cues, whereas processing them through separate streams may fail to coordinate them. Second, insufficient personalized adaptation in progressive SID decisions: although decoder states evolve with generated prefixes, existing models typically use a shared output-side transformation across recommendation instances, without explicitly selecting a transformation suited to the current user need. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation (MV-Thinker), a framework that Thinks Globally and Generates Personally. First, Multi-View Temporal Thinking uses view-specific thinking queries and readers over overlapping full-history and recent-history views, coordinating both sources into complementary user-conditioned contexts before SID generation. Second, Hierarchical Residual Adaptation organizes lightweight adapters into nested residual paths before a shared vocabulary projection, adaptively transforming context-bearing decoder states for SID decisions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that MV-Thinker consistently outperforms strong discriminative and generative recommendation baselines across multiple ranking metrics. The implementation code and datasets are available on: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MV-Thinker
papers.summary: A user's full history and their last few actions describe the same person, but they give different signals. Putting everything into one sequence dilutes the recent interest, while two separate streams fail to line up with each other. MV-Thinker uses one shared set of learnable query vectors with two independent readers to read the full history and the recent history separately. Because both sides use the same queries, their outputs line up one to one while each keeps its own long-term or recent information, and only then does SID generation start. Across four public datasets and two SID construction methods, it beats both discriminative and generative baselines. This is an academic architecture improvement with no online validation yet.

papers.title: Beyond Uniform Token Training: A Multi-Target Framework for Learning Token-Weighted Objectives in Generative Recommenders
papers.authors: Wei-Ning Chiu, Song-Duo Ma, H. Shu, Chuan‐Ju Wang, Pu‐Jen Cheng
papers.abstract: Recent generative recommendation models recast next-item prediction as the generation of a semantic identifier sequence. While this formulation enables autoregressive models to produce item IDs directly, the commonly used token-level likelihood objective does not distinguish between tokens that play different roles in item identification. This limitation is especially pronounced for semantic-ID representations, where prefix tokens often determine coarse item groups and later tokens provide finer-grained disambiguation. To better align training with the structure of semantic IDs, we study token-level learning signals from two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a prefix-aware weighting scheme, Front-Greater Weighting, which emphasizes tokens according to their contribution to reducing semantic ambiguity among candidate items. Second, frequency weighting increases the learning emphasis on infrequent tokens, addressing the long-tailed distributions and popularity bias commonly observed in recommendation data. We further introduce a multi-target optimization framework with curriculum learning, which integrates the two token-weighted objectives with the standard likelihood and enables stable optimization with adaptive emphasis across training stages. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves generative recommendation performance over strong baselines and prior token-weighting methods. Additional analyses show that the method is robust across different semantic-ID constructions and backbone scales, and that it improves recommendation quality for both popular and long-tail items. Code is available at github repository.

papers.summary: Generative recommenders are trained with the same loss weight on every SID token, and this paper finds that weighting tokens by position and rarity reliably improves recommendations. The reason is that the first few positions of an SID decide the broad item group, the later ones only refine it, and some tokens are very rare. This paper adds two kinds of token weights. One looks at position: the more candidate items a position rules out once it is fixed, the larger its weight, so earlier positions weigh more. The other looks at frequency: the less often a token appears in the training data, the larger its weight. During training it optimizes these two weighted losses together with the ordinary likelihood loss. Compared with the base TIGER model, Hit@5 improves 6.11% on average, and both popular and long-tail items get better. ==It only changes loss weights, not the model architecture==, so the cost of adopting it is low.

papers.title: Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation with Sibling Alignment for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Rongfeng Guo, Zhuang Zhuang, Ji Dai, Peng Zhao, Shijie Li, Jie Chen, Teng Long, Vincent Tao Hu, Fei Pan
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs, typically via beam search. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enhances training supervision by transferring privileged self-teacher knowledge at student-generated states. However, beam-search retention depends on competition among prefixes: visited states differ in importance, and initially reliable decisions may approach the pruning boundary as training evolves. Moreover, conventional distribution matching couples target-token confidence with preferences among competing continuations, potentially weakening relational supervision when the self-teacher strongly favors the target. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (SA-OPSD), a framework that transfers privileged self-teacher knowledge to the states visited during the student's own beam search. Specifically, we introduce Evolving-Boundary Sampling, which prioritizes search-critical states by considering both current pruning-boundary proximity and initial-reference retention-margin decline under a controlled distillation budget. Furthermore, we develop Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation, which separates target-probability calibration from informative sibling relations to better preserve the teacher's preferences among competing branches. Experiments on Industrial, Office, and Instruments demonstrate strong performance for SA-OPSD.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders produce results with beam search, and a pruned prefix can never come back, yet common self-distillation training ignores which prefixes are about to be pruned. The teacher in self-distillation is a frozen copy of the same model that also sees the target item's title during training, and it supervises every state the student generates equally. SA-OPSD distills only on the states the student's own beam search visits, and favors states whose scores sit closest to the beam's cutoff line, the ones that are close to being pruned. It does better on one industrial and two public datasets, trains at lower cost than full KL distillation, and leaves inference unchanged.

papers.title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuohang Jiang, Yuxin Chen, Haohao Qu, ZeFei luo, Yunlong Wang, Xu Yuan, Haojie Ding, Boheng Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongyang Wang, Jun Wang, Zhongbo Sun, Wenqi Fan, Li Qing, Wenwu Ou, Peng Jiang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders are trained only on interaction data and make little use of the semantic knowledge already inside large language models. The beam search likelihood ranks token sequences, which is not the same as how relevant an item is to a user. HiGenTrans brings LLM knowledge in at three places. Before generation, it adds an LLM-computed user representation to the start of the sequence. In the middle layers, it pulls each layer of the generative model toward the LLM layer at the same relative depth. At the end, a small MoE scorer combines semantic relevance, generation confidence and candidate-set information to rerank the beam search output. All semantic features are computed only from the user's existing interactions and can be cached offline. On three public datasets, NDCG@10 improves by up to 33.7%, and on every dataset NDCG rises more than Recall, so the gain mostly comes from ranking the right items higher.

papers.title: Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines
papers.authors: Guanrong Li, Haolin Yang, Xinyu Liu, Zhen Wu, Rui Xia
papers.abstract: In the era of generative AI, recommender systems are moving from precise prediction to trustworthy generation. Large language models (LLMs) support this shift by inferring user interests and producing natural-language explanations. However, LLM-based recommendation suffers from a fundamental obstacle: popularity bias. Through pre-training on massive corpora, LLMs tend to rely on global statistics and trend signals, yielding recommendations that follow popularity rather than genuine preference. As this bias is entangled in model parameters and is hard to remove directly, we propose Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines (NPRec), a model-agnostic framework that mitigates popularity bias through external semantic intervention. NPRec performs counterfactual refinement to causally separate intrinsic user interests from popularity-driven conformity, producing debiased textual guidelines that reflect actual user preferences. These guidelines are injected at inference time to shift the LLM from unconstrained generation to guided reasoning, without any parameter updates. Serving as explicit premises, they both ground faithful explanations and improve recommendation quality. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NPRec achieves promising performance in recommendation accuracy, explanation quality, and debiasing capability.

papers.summary: When a large language model makes recommendations, it often follows the popularity it learned in pre-training, recommending what is popular rather than what this user likes. This bias lives in the parameters and is hard to remove directly. NPRec leaves the parameters untouched. It first generates several candidate text guidelines from the user's interactions, each describing a possible preference. It then trains a small model that predicts whether a guideline applies to a given user and item. Each guideline gets two such probabilities, one with the real user and item, and one with the user and item inputs both replaced by all-zero vectors so only item popularity remains. Only guidelines whose first probability is clearly higher are kept, since one that applies on popularity alone is really about following the crowd. At inference the guideline goes into the prompt, so the model recommends and explains by following it. With guidelines written by people, the top-1 hit rate on MovieLens beats basic prompting by 95.6%. ==How good the guideline is matters most==.
